lg.l: [The confidante] entrusting [the heroine to the hero], [the hero's] joy, the speech of the onlookers,
the speech of the distressed foster-mother to the birth-mother,
[the foster-mother] weeping about [the couple] going through the desert, the onlookers clarifying [the situation],Alternatively removing her distress (see TNV22).
[the foster-mother] returning,This situation does not receive an example poem in the commentary. the young men [of her family] going [after them],
[the hero] knowing [they are coming and] hiding, the neighbours speaking,
[the hero] who had left, returning [with her], the joy of [the heroine's] many relatives,
the speech of the mothers, the speech of the hero

div.p: The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which 'the elopement' occurs.
kai yaṭai mutal ākat talaimakaṉ kūṟṟīṟākac collap paṭṭaṉa varaivu maṟuttuḻi yākiya vuṭaṉ celavām eṉṟa vāṟu.
Beginning with entrusting and ending with the speech of the hero — those things which have been mentioned are the elopement which takes place after the marriage rejection.

lg.l: Without you, she is nothing.ivaḷē niṉ alatu ilaḷē has also been understood as, “Without you, she has no one”, (See Buck and Paramasivan).
And without her with kajal eyes like waterlilies, mother is nothing.
I am in that situation as well!
O man from the land with great mountains, please don't forget!

div.p: [The confidante] entrusting [the heroine to the hero].

lg.l: Softly, softly, you innocent girl, with your gait,niṉ naṭai āṟṟi literally translates to either, “carrying/bearing your gait, go...”, or, “your gait being able to bear it, go...”. The first interpretation requires no subject-change which makes it preferable.
go without suffering along the path
which we will travel to the cool dark grove.poḻila is understood here as an adjectival form qualifying āṟu. Theoretically, this could also be a neuter plural pronominalised noun.

div.p: The speech of the hero's joy.

lg.l: Will you rejoice when you see,kāṇṭiyō: this subjunctive + -ō formulation is a late-Caṅkam development found first in the Kalittokai. I understand it as a conditional question ('Would/will you x if/when y'), but it is not widely attested and I am not totally convinced of this interpretation, though I do think it makes sense here. For a disuccion on the variant reading, see the critical notes opposite. O heart,
the beauty of the peacock-nature of the woman with dark hair

who you did not reach even though you climbedIt is not clear what this refers to. Did they have to physically climb over a barrier to try and meet the heroine, or is this metaphorical, refering to one's spirits being raised? ivarntaṉai could also be translated as, 'you desired' according to the TL, but this is not a meaning attested in the Caṅkam corpus. and went after her yesterday.
After I sent her ahead saying,
and stroked [your] beautiful body and hair,
I shall see your dainty back."
she became shy and hung back to hide and because I also hung back,

won't we now be delayedvaikiṉa-mātō... paruvattāṉē literally translates to, “won't we be delayed with regards to the season.” One has to understand that 'the season' is the season of their return. paruvam is regularly used to refer to the opportune/appropriate time for something. along with [her] hips with an expanded hood.pai viri alkul is unambiguously referring to the heroine's vulva and clitoral hood. Whether or not one ought to translate alkul as 'vulva' is up for debate (See Wilden). At this stage of the language, it had come to regularly refer to the waist/hips.
The man with the bow has anklets on his legs
and the girl with bangles has anklets above her soft feet.
Who are [those] good ones? They are pitiable indeed!
These people who are approaching the thickets of denseOr, 'rustling bamboo'. bamboo
where the white Sirissa tree nuts sound out after the wind hits them
so they beat like the drums of the rope dancing Āriyar.

div.p: Those who encounter [the couple] in the desert speak.

lg.l: The hot one who travels with red rays has also joined with the road.There are two potential interpretations for how this could refer to sunset, which it does: either the sun joins with the road in the sense that it meets where the road crosses meets the horizon, thereby setting, or it joins with its path, i.e. it goes along it prescribed route, thereby setting.

After you have stayed hereMy impression is that the poet regularly uses ivvaḻi to mean, 'here'. One could translate it more literally, as has been done in other translations presented in this edition, as, “along this way.” [for the night]
with the girl whose hair is full of pollen,

leave, O worthy one!The point of the poem is that the onlookers are warning the hero from continuing along this dangerous road through the wilderness. They point out that even the sun has retired for the night, implying that the hero ought to do the same and spend the night with them before returning home. The muṟṟeccam phrase, taṅkiṉai ceṉmō has been translated here similarly to if taṅkutal were an absolutive. More literally one could translate: “Leave as one who has stayed here”.
O brahmin, I worship you! Tell them,
Going as oneI.e. 'together with'. with the young man with the tall chariot,
she crossed the harsh desert without harm."
so that the great sorrow of the mother and friends perishes
when they become agitated by the waning moon.It is not clear what specific importance the waning moon has. Perhaps this is simply a for a nicer turn of phrase.

div.p: The heroine speaks to an onlooker.

lg.l: And now, without seeing the girl with arms

where bangles spreadvār is very polysemous. This phrase could also be translated: “arms with bangles arranged in order (i.e. regularly)”, “arms with bangles that flow down [them]”, “arms overflowing with bangles” etc. and hair around which bees buzz
in the places where she used to play, how do you exist,niṉṟaṉai-kollō is more literally, 'how do you stand', but it often carries the sense of existence.
embracing a body no longer there, O heart?

div.p: [The foster mother] speaks about not seeing the heroine and weeps.

lg.l: O, you are stong indeed! Even though you stayed behind,
after your beloved friend with shining bangles departed,kai is understood as a verbal prefix here, but one could also take it as a noun, in which case: “after your beloved friend's hand departed.”
you are still united with your life and feel no distress.

div.p: The foster mother sees the confidante and speaks [to her].

lg.l: After the surrounding and darkening clouds flash,
let the harshness of the wilderness leave as it showers on the road
along which you with the doe-like kajal eyes go.

div.p: On realising the heroine has gone, the birth-mother weeps.

lg.l: O small black crow with faultless feathers!
In my tradition of kindness, don't I bring fresh meat
poured onto freshly boiled rice grainspacum tiṉai puṉkam can also mean: “freshly boiled milled and rice...”

in an ornate gold pot so that your family grow.Either this refers to them literally swelling up from the quantity of food they are provided, or that they grow stronger (possibly in number) from her repeated gifts.
Please call out to the girl with pretty fine hair so she comes back
with the young man of hot anger and a victorious spear!
He did not dig up and enter the ground,
he did not rise up into the sky,
and he did not walk intoOr: “walk towards”. the dark shining ocean.
If we search land by land, town by town, home by home,

will he really stayThe um in keṭunarum is not so clear. It is interpreted here as an eccavummai. The co-ordintaion is with the list of things that he has not done, but in practise, this has a sense that he will not be able to evade them if they search for him, hence it is translated as a rhetorical question. lost, our lover?

div.p: eṉpatu naṟṟāykkuc collic cevili piṉ ceṉṟatu.
The foster mother speaks to the birth-mother then goes [after the couple].

lg.l: When the arrows shot from the bow of the cruel man pierced it,
In this very place where the girl with the bangles stepped,

so that her string of ornaments from which pearls were discardedThere are different ways to split the sandhi here and construe the line. First, on can either read, viṭu muttu..., as in the translation presented, or iṭu muttu... — 'ornamented string with inset pearls'. There is then also the question of what exactly the agent of cuṭara is — the string or the pearls? Syntax suggests the string, common sense the pearls. glow.

div.p: The foster mother, who has gone into the desert, weeps.

lg.l: Surely you are angry and hostile [to me],

O Kuravu tree holding up beautiful dolls,As one can see in the PK sources supplied, the idea here is that the 'dolls' are the young flowers of the tree. The point is that the tree also has experience with parenthood, so it should have known to stop the heroine and should also understand the foster-mother's pain.
as the one with the eminent jewels has alsoIn addition to me, the foster-mother. gone though the hot fiery desert.
You brahmins with fine cords around your chests,
did you see a woman with bright jewels going through the harsh desert
with a majestic man whose power shines, or other people?

div.p: eṉpatu cevili yiṭaic curattu varuvārai viṉāyiṟṟu.
The foster mother questions those who have come from the desert.

lg.l: O, please don't suffer on account of the foolish girl.
Love for those people who have pearls produced from the belly of the ocean
is the natural way of the world.

div.p: eṉpatu ceviliyai yiṭaic curattuk kaṇṭōr teruṭṭiyatu.
The onlookers inform [the couple] the foster mother about the middle of the desert.

lg.l: Does she think of me too?
My daughter who crossed many luscious hills
so that gossip rose up in the noisy ancient village

with the young man who swore an oath to eat her heart.The is the option to read the phrase, neñcu uṇa tēṟṟiya vañciṉam kāḷaiyoṭu differently. tēṟṟutal can also mean 'to assure', or something similar. So: “with the young man of an oath, who assured her in order to eat her heart.”

div.p: The foster mother returns to the house.

lg.l: Those bowmen bent low from shameThis could either be shame on account of her actions, or, “men with bent bows for the sake of [her] modesty”. are her relatives
and they are coming here in anger.
When they encircle [them], what will become of them [two]?Presumably, they are wondering about the fate of the couple, not the relatives pursuing them.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṭamar piṉ cellak kaṇṭār colliyatu.
The onlookers speak about the heroine's relatives going after [the couple].

lg.l: Your relatives have arrows which resemble spears.
In the shade around the mountain pool

densely packed with flowers that are clasped and curved,Alternatively, kayil vaḷai could mean 'curved like a clasp' or that they are 'curved and intelocking'. See my upcoming article for an exhaustive discussion of the options.
I will hide for a little while, O one with the grace of a peacock.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṭamar ātal aṟintu talaimakaṉ maṟaintatu.
The hero learns of the existence of the heroine's relatives [trailing them] and hides.

lg.l: Lifting up their lines of bows on their left and checking their arrows,
these people have eyes that shoot fire.
And now, we shall inform the people who know the waytiṟaṉ can also mean 'the issue', in which case: “the people who know what is going on”.
by telling them, "In between anger and the tall distant lord
who hid, thinking of the relatives of the woman with beautiful jewels,
there is no virtue.This is a metaphorical way to say that there is no virtue in fighting.

div.p: The onlookers speak about the middle of the desert.

lg.l: She is the one whose love excels in goodness.
He is the son of worthy people from an excellent family.
Looking at both of their natures, is it not natural
to give [her for marriage] without being afflicted?Lit., “without reaching/obtaining affliction.”
O my love with perfect graceful hips, let us hurry
and reach the largeviyal normally means 'width'. Describing a house as wide essentially means it is large or great. great old abode so that our relatives

who have borne such great affliction, sway from joy.This is a play of the double-meaning of makiḻ, which either means 'joy' or 'toddy'. In the second option, her relatives will be swaying because they are drunk after celebrating.
When you hasten and go to those people who are like life [to me]
and who have love in their hearts [for me], say,
"They are coming back from the fertile forest today."
They say that she will come along the small road

from the mountainOne can either understand malai mutal ciṟu neṟi as 'a small path beginning at the mountain', as in this translation, or as, 'a small path from the base of the mountain.' where deer confuse the pathsThis signifies that the area is difficult to navigate and therefore dangerous.
— the girl with the broad soft shoulders, carefully, carefully stepping,
as her feet, soft as cotton, are wounded by the gravel.

div.p: Her relatives learn [they are] coming back and rejoice.

lg.l: Tell us, O Vēlaṉ of ancient knowledge,
the intentions of his majesty with a shining spear
towards the young woman with hair overflowing with nectar.

div.p: The foster mother questions the priest.

lg.l: AndThe function of the -um on koṇṭum is unclear. It presumably co-ordinates with something not mentioned in the poem. [you], understanding her abandonment, O mother with difficult blemishes,
who, emaciated from the torment of affliction, angrily blames virtue,
has your daughter come back to delight your troubled heart,
led by a hot powerful warrior with a shining spear?

div.p: The foster mother speaks to the birth-mother.

lg.l: Alas! This is not the way!
Come and show love to the mother
who has lost her sense of selfThis the rendering of niṟai, which conveys a sense of fulfilment or self-control.
and bears an affliction of deep despair.

div.p: The hero's birth-mother speaks to the hero.

lg.l: O friend, what if we told the mother who begot the young man
with faultless shining anklets on his legs
"Although her anklet was removed in your house,
let the wedding and good marriage take place in ours!"

div.p: The foster mother speaks to the heroine's birth-mother.

lg.l: O you who entered the protectedkaṭi maṉai is either a 'protected' or 'fragrant' home. Considering this poem is describing a wedding scene, the latter would make sense sense, however kaṭi maṉai is a term used to refer to the post-marriage home. Cf. NA40.1, Kali44.9 and the kiḷavi to Aink401-10. home
while the women of ancient knowledge

adoringlyparavu-tal could also, in this context, be translated as extensively if one takes it to be intransitive. praised the newly dressed bride and her beauty,This could either refer to her natural beauty, or to the beauty of her make-up and costume (cf. TNV17-38)
did you have any idea [this would happen]
back at our meeting-place on the slopes where pepper grows?

div.p: The hero speaks to the heroine.

standOff.note: Cf. TP40n.8-9: ceynilaik kakaṉṟōr celaviṉum varaviṉuṅ | kaṇṭōr moḻital kaṇṭa teṉpa ||
Cf. TP506n.2: kaṇṭōr moḻital kaṇṭa teṉpa ||
Cf. TP193i.3-4: ...kaṇṭōr | yātta ciṟappiṉ vāyilka ḷeṉpa ||

In all of the sources cited, the additional information in the cūttiram either enumerates the people allowed to act as intermediaries, the people to whom the onlookers can speak or about what they can speak. They are not listed in full as the TNV cūttiram does not provide this information. Also note that these could equally well function as a source for the speech-situation spoken by the onlookers in line three.

This reading aligns with the koḷu in the commentary, so it is presumably the reading known to the commentator. It was no possible to find malaital as a sub-situation in other poetic treatises, so this edition deviates from the MS reading.

Likewise, this aligns with what the koḷu suggests was the text known to the commentator. The transmission here is rather odd though. The palm-leaf MS gives different readings in the mūlam and commentary. Additionally, UVC in the first edition of the text, printed talaimakaṉ in the mūlam, talaimakaḷ in the short prose commentary and then talaimakaṉ again in the koḷu. These readings are normalised to talaimakaṉ, deviating from the MS, as it is unambiguous that the speaker of the poem cited in the commentary is the hero. This situation is also not found in other treatises so there is no other information upon which to base this decision.
Cf. AV182.9: kaiyatai koṭuttal
Cf. AV182.10: avaṉcurat tuyttal
Cf. AV182.11: uvarntalar cūṭṭi uṇmakiḻn turaittal

The AV commentary cites NA9 for the first situation cited above, which is the source for the poem provided for this situation in the TNV, hence why it is included even though the koḷu here does not show any similarity to the AV parallel.

The second AV parallel more closely resembles the koḷu, so it is provided here, even though it more closely describes the situation found in the fourth poem cited for this cūttiram in the TNV, which is given the same koḷu.
Cf. AV182.12: kaṇṭō rayirttal
The AV commentary cites this same poem to exemplify this situation. It is not included in the apparatus as Wilden 2010 reports that information.
Cf. AV184.3: taṉṉaṟi viṉmai taṉṉainon turaittal

On every occasion colli is found in a TNV koḷu, it is preceded by either āka (see, TNV 17, koḷu 13 and 32, for example), or a dative to mark the addressee of the poem (TNV23, koḷu 12). UVC's emendation solves the problem that C1 satisfied neither of these criteria. It also follows the wider pattern of the koḷu-s in this section of the text (and the TNV in general, though this is not a universal feature of the koḷu-s - see introduction, section x), where the speaker is stated. This is a likelier reading than that transmitted in C1̇.
Cf. AV184.1-2: viṉaviya pāṅkiyi ṉuṇarnta kālai | iṉaiya leṉpōrk ketiraḻintu moḻital
Cf. AV184.4: teyvam vaḻttal
The AV commentary cites KT378 for this situation, which is the source material for the poem cited in the TNV.
Cf. AV188.1: āṟṟāt tāyait tēṟṟal
Cf. AV188.4: cuvaṭukaṇ ṭiraṅkal
Cf. AV188.4: kuravoṭu pulampal
The second situation cited from the AV corresponds to the next poem cited in the TNV. It is cited here as the TNV doesn't differentiate between the two situations.
Cf. AV188.5: kalantuṭaṉ varuvōrk kaṇṭukēṭ ṭal
Cf. AV188.5-6: avar | pulampal tēṟṟal
kaṇṭōr is the well-established terminology for 'the onlookers' the couple encounter in the desert (Cf. TP494i.2, cited as a source for TNV23).
Cf. AV198.4-6: ...īṉṟāṭ | aṟattoṭu niṟṟaliṟ ṟamarpiṉ cēralait | talaivi kaṇṭu talaivaṟ kuṇarttal
Cf. AV191.3-4: talaivimuṉ celvōr tammoṭu taṉvaral | pāṅkiyark kuṇartti viṭuttal
Cf. AV191.6-7: naṟṟāy kēṭṭavaṉ | uḷaṅkōḷ vēlaṉai viṉātal
Cf. AV194.3-4: varaintamai cevili | naṟṟāyk kuṇarttal
Cf. AV194.1-2: paṇimoḻi naṟṟāy maṇaṉayar vēṭkaiyiṟ | ceviliyai viṉātal
There is a formula adj + malai + nāṭaṉ. I found no instance where malai nāṭan is not preceded by a qualifier.

This poem is anonymous but almost certainly predates the TNV, as it is found in the IAC. There is no reason to think the C1 readings, which in any case do not make good sense in the context of the speech situtaion, were the poet's composition. The reading ilaṉē in the first line, for example, requires the heroine to be the addressee, in which case the vocative in the last line - nāṭa, which is one the standard terms of address for the hero - would not make sense. The poem is widely quoted and the text is stable. C1 looks like a corrupted outlier.
Cf. PK184.1 (IAC23, p.163): paṇtāṉa ṉaiyacol vāypaiya vēku
Cf. PK185.4 (IAC23, p.163): nāi yātu naṭakkave ṉaṉṉutalē ||
Cf. NA9.9-12 (IAC23, p.153): varuntā tēkumati vāleyiṟ ṟōyē | mānaṉai koḻuti makiḻkuyi lālu | naṟuntaṇ poḻila kāṉaṅ | kuṟumpa lūrayāñ cellu māṟē ||
Cf. TK215.1: pēṇat tiruttiya cīṟaṭi mellaccel

I hesitate to chose KKms and UVC's reading of nallaṭi ('good feet'), which makes perfect sense. I have not found any other convincing parallels in the old corpus which would suggest this reading, and I would argue the C1 reading is as sensible. UVC may have agreed, as this is one of only four variants which he notes in his edition. Without another parallel, I do not see the need to deviate from C1.

Even though one finds the root imperative ēku in both C1 and PK184, it is highly likely that the source and point of reference for the poet here was NA9, where we find the phrase - varuntātu ēkumati. One might argue that this well known parallel might have influenced a scribe and caused an error, but in the context of the poem the polite imperative ending in -mati appropriate. It is also supported by G1, though in this case I did not consider that evidence too stongly. NA9 and this TNV a quoted on after the other, and this would have been an easy mistake to make. Overall though, the close parallel convinces me to adopt UCV's emended reading.

One can make good sense of both readings here, possibly even better sense of UVC's emendation. He replaces the interoggative particle with a emphatic, so: "O, you shall rejoice when you see..." His emendation requires minimal intervention - one must delete only one kāl. However, the C1 reading is also perfectly plausible and we find more evidence for subjunctive + -ō forms in the old corpus. Indeed in Kali129.14, there is a parralel construction: aṟintaṉai naraṟiyō. I did not find such instances with the emphatic particle -ē, so this edition reverts to the C1 reading.

Cf. AN261: kāṉap pātiri karuntakaṭ ṭoḷvī | vēṉi latiraloṭu viraiik kāṇvarac | cilaiṅ kūnta laḻutti melliṇart | tēmpāy marāa maṭaicci vāṉkō | lilaṅkuvaḷai teḷirppa vīcic cilampunakac | ciṉamel lotukkamoṭu meṉmela viyaliniṉ | ṉaṇimāṇ ciṟupuṟaṅ kāṇkañ ciṟunaṉi | yēkeṉa vēka ṉāṇi yoyyeṉa | māko ṇōkkamoṭu maṭaṅkoḷac cāay | niṉṟutalai yiṟaiñci yōḷē yatukaṇ | ṭiyāmun tuṟutal cellē māyiṭai | yaruñcurat talki yēmē yirumpuli | kaḷiṟaṭṭuk kuḻumu mōcaiyuṅ kaḷipaṭṭu | villōr kuṟumpiṟ ṟatumpum | valvāyk kaṭuntuṭip pāṇiyum kēṭṭē ||

Cf. TK219: aṉpaṇait tañcolli piṉcellu māṭava ṉīṭavaṉṟaṉ | piṉpaṇait tōḷi varumip peruñcurañ celvataṉṟu | poṉpaṇait taṉṉa viṟaiyuṟai tillaip polimalarmēl | naṉpaṇait taṇṇaṟa vuṇṇaḷi pōṉṟoḷir nāṭakamē ||

Both readings can make sense here — the couple are delayed with regard to their return in C1, though the final tāṉē is awkward, and delayed in the wilderness in the others. This edition opts for the print reading on the strength of the AN source and TK parallel. In both poems, there is explicit mention of the couple staying in the wilderness. ṟ and ḻ sound similar and so it is plausible that a scribe may have confused the two at some point.

The C1 reading is almost certainly corrupt, though one can make sense of it. It is not found in any manuscript or edition which prints this poem, including where it is quoted in commentaries to other text (such as in the case of the TNV). The KT mirrors the construction of the following phrase nicely - the hero wears warrior anklets on his legs, and the heroine has anklets above her feet. For poetic reasons, this reading is preferable. The C1 reading is also syntactically more awkward. The only way to make sense of reading villōṉ kāval kaḻalē involves inverting the natural word-order, placing the attribute - 'being watchful' or 'keeping guard' after the subject. This would translate to: "The man with the bow, keeping watch, [wears] warrior anklets".
Cf. PK186.3-4 (IAC23, p.164): malaimaṉṉum veyyōṉ maṟaintaṉaṉ mātumey vāṭinaintāḷ | cilaimaṉṉu tōḷaṇṇal cērntaṉai celleñ ciṟukuṭikkē ||
Cf. PK187.2-4 (IAC23, p.164): mikamelintāḷ | kuṉṟār cuṭarōṉ maṟaintaṉaṉ kūrvēl viṭalaitaṅkic | ceṉṟā laḻivatuṇ ṭōvaṇit toleñ ciṟukuṭiyē ||

UVC's emendation here is reasonable. Something with the sense of 'join the road' is what one expects in the final two cīr-s of line one. This is a common euphamism to say the sun has set. That is the clear intention of the poet. There is text-internal evidence for this as well. One finds an almost identical phrase in TNV18, poem 3, line 1 : āykatirc celva ṉattañ cērnteṉa. There is no variant reading for the final cīr. If one wanted to argue for the C1 reading as the lectio difficilior, then there is a way to make sense of it. The sun would have 'laid down on the road' or 'reddened'. The first option could also work as euphamisms for sunset, though neither fit the more common formula, supported by the TNV parallel.
Cf. Aiṅk384: cēṭpula muṉṉiya vacainaṭai yantaṇir | nummoṉ ṟirantaṉeṉ moḻiva lemmūr | yāynayan teṭutta vāynalaṅ kaviṉa | vāriṭai yiṟantaṉa ḷeṉmi | ṉēriṟai muṉkaiyeṉ ṉāyat tōrkkē ||

One does not expect gemination following a vocative, which antaṇir, although it is unmarked, is.

There is no question that varivaḷai tōḷi ('she with arms with rows of bangles') is a common formula, and possibly this is why UVC changed this reading. There is also one other instance of this phrase in TNV18, poem 11. However, in this case, I do not condier that good enough reason to discount C1's semantically and metrically sound version. One can also find this phrase, or something almost identical, twice in the Peruṅkaṭai. See 3:10:24 and 5:3:125. This is a very marginal case.

I am not clear why UVC emended here. C1 preserves the alliteration on the third and fourth consonants of final two lines. pētuṟṟilai is also a perfectly acceptable form for a negative, affixing -il, with a prononminal ending, onto the past stem of the compound verb pētu-uṟu-tal. This form was not present in the oldest strata of Tamil, but by now would have been used frequently (Wilden 2018: 147).

This emendation seems unnecessary. I assume UVC edited the text in line with the end of KT378, which was a clear source for the poem. It is not, however, a hard and fast rule that the poet copied phrases from the source material when referncing them, and I would argue that the C1 reading here makes perfect sense, and that there is no convincing reason to think a scribe would have mistakenly switched a word the phrase known from a similar famous poem - curaṉ - out for neṟi, which also bears no orthographic similarity.

Presumably UVC preferred to read a short i because of kaṇṭaṉir in line 3, which I do not feel is necessary. Both forms are equally acceptable and fit the metre. It is also not a requirement for there to be perfect synchronicity between the verbal and nominal endings. For example, in Kali9 the predicate for antaṇīr is kāṇirō.

Whether to read piṟavōr (C2), or piṟavō (C1) is a marginal case. The latter option would translate to: “did you see the girl... or other things?”. Neither option ahs an exact parallel anywhere, though Kali9.8 might give a small clue. In the same poetic context, the question is asked, aṉṉār iruvarai kāṇirō, 'did you see two people like these?'. There is no suggestion that the object of the brahmin's sight would be anything apart from a human, thus in this poem a neuter plural would not be expected.

The C1 reading, also found in the Ain editions I consulted makes perfect sense, so UVC must have had a good reason to modify it. I can only assume that reason was access to and/or familiarity with a different version of the poem fro what I have seen.

C1 would require a form ceḻu, which I would argue only exists hypothetically. There are no instances where this adjectival form of the abstract noun ceḻumai drops its -m-, apart from when followed by a word with an initial nasal, which is a feature of sandhi and could equally be dissolved as ceḻu or ceḻum. In all other cases the attested form is ceḻum, and there are attestations of ceḻumpal in the old corpus (KT287.7, for example). In support of the hypothetical exitence of ceḻu pal is the attested collocation ciṟu pal (AN137.2, NA181.5 for example), where ciṟu is the adjectival form of the abstract noun ciṟumai. However, without any attestation, the evidence is not strong enough to retain the C1 reading.

I follow UVC here. One can just about make sense of the reading in C1, but were that to have been the original text, it would be a unique formation in the corpus. ivvaḷaiyāk kālē necessitates taking vaḷai as a noun, as it is preceded by a deictic. This would then leave ā, which has to be a verbal root functioning as a peyareccam, as kāl, when used in such a construction to mean 'when...', is always preceded by a peyareccam. Nowhere else in the corpus is the preceding peyareccam a verbal root. If one were to translate it, the final line would read: "When they (the bowmen) are in these surroundings, what will become of them [the couple or the bowmen]?" In UVC's proposed emedation vaḷaiyum is a non-past peyareccam and ivar is its subject. Theoretically, one could read vaḷaiyā as a negative peyareccam, but in that case the poem would not make sense. A non-past peyareccam is the only reasonable option and ivar is as minimal and as plausible an emendation possible.

I follow UVC here. The C1 reading makes as good sense as the emended reading found in C2pc onwards, but it is unlikely that this was the reading. Both āy iḻai and ari iḻai mean something close to 'beautiful jewels'. The former is an extremely common collocation occurring dozens of times in the Caṅkam corpus alone and three other times in the TNV (TNV 15, poem 4; TNV16, poem 7; TNV 18, poem 8), whereas there is no evidence ari iḻai. Perhaps a scribe untintenttionally miscopied or incorrectly corrected the kāl marking the long ā for a with a ri. This woudl only require the addition one extra vowel mark - the two readings are orthogrpahically very similar. Reading ari also maintains the same etukai from the first two lines, which may be the underlying reason behing the error. Reading āy, however allows for a sort-of-etukai, or at least a shared rhythmic pattern between lines three and four, giving the stanza an AABBCC-type construction. Such metrical arguments should not be considered strong evidence to support on reading over another in this text (see introduction, section X), but they can explain previousl editorial choices or occurrences (in the case of unintentional or subconcious changes). Since āy iḻai is so common and is found in other TNV poems, and since the is a potential reason why C1's corrupted reading may hve snuck in, I think there is justification to deviate from the manuscript.

This is also a reasonable emendation to make. Reading the poem as presented in C1, one can make sense of it. The only thing one would have to change from the translation on the opposite page is the fist line. I would understand vēḷē as an akupeyar for the heroine - 'the desirous one'. The syntax and meaning of the rest of the poem would remain identical. The problem is that vēḷē is not found elsewhere used in this way. Reading ivaḷē also provides a nice, logical counterpart to ivaṉē at the end of the line. Orthographically, these two readings are also close. In palm-leaf MSS, the sign for an initial i- can often resemble a kompu, used to mark e/ē. See, for example, how they look in C1: i- Sign for initial i- and a kompu kompu diacritic from C1. Mistaking one for the other is the only difference between the two readings. I believe this was a simple scribal error.

Understanding the C1 reading hinges on two pre-requisites: first, understanding the -ō particle as either a focaliser, marking the addressee, or as a kind of particle of lament appended to a functional vocative; second, that that the whole of the second line is a aṉmoḻittokai for the heroine - "O, [my] love with perfect, graceful hips". UVC may have thought such a compound was unlikely, as one does not find other instances of naṭpu in this usage. A more common phrase to refer to the woman is (positive quality) + alkul. If this phrase is the 'vocative', then emending naṭpō is necessary to construe the poem, and UVS's suggestions make sense, with the initial emendation in C2pc being the least violent. I see no need to fully replace the word as in Cām. without a compelling textual parallel, which there is not. For some semantic reasons why he might have found naṭpu suspicious and my reasons why I do not, see the notes to the translation.
